statement: The Greek alphabet derives from Phoenician, c. 800-700 BCE, with a genuine structural innovation: the Greeks repurposed several Phoenician consonantal signs representing sounds absent from Greek (glottal/pharyngeal consonants — aleph, he, yod, ayin) as dedicated vowel letters (alpha, epsilon, iota, omicron), producing the first script with systematic vowel notation, distinct from Semitic matres lectionis (partial/optional vowel indication). Named authorities: Roger D. Woodard (grapheme-adaptation detail) and Barry B. Powell (argues the adaptation was purpose-driven, tied to recording Homeric epic). A live epigraphic debate exists over exactly how early/where transmission occurred, but the ~800 BCE date and the vowel-innovation mechanism itself are not contested.
